items.title: UK GDPR, Article 6: Lawfulness of processing
items.locator: Art. 6(1)(a) to (f), 6(5) and 6(11); notes F3 and F14
items.quote: processing is necessary for the purposes of a recognised legitimate interest
items.why: The binding rule: processing is lawful only if at least one listed basis applies. Point (ea) was inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s.70(2)(b), in force 19 June 2025 for specified purposes and 5 February 2026 otherwise (S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(c)). Points (ea) and (f) are not open to public authorities performing their tasks. Banner on the date checked: no known outstanding effects.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22B: Restrictions on automated decision-making
items.quote: is carried out entirely or partly in reliance on Article 6(1)(ea)
items.why: The exclusion: a significant decision may not be taken solely by automated processing where the processing for it relies, wholly or partly, on recognised legitimate interests. It is limited to solely automated decisions. Inserted by the 2025 Act, s.80(1); in force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(j)).

items.title: UK GDPR, Annex 1: Lawfulness of processing: recognised legitimate interests
items.quote: This condition is met where the processing is necessary for the purposes of responding to an emergency.
items.why: The closed list behind the new basis: disclosure to a body with a public task; national security, public security and defence; emergencies; crime; safeguarding vulnerable individuals. Nothing in it covers model training or commercial AI use. Inserted 5 February 2026 by the 2025 Act, Sch. 4 (S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(z6)).

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 8A: Purpose limitation: further processing
items.locator: Art. 8A(2) and (3); note F1. Read with Art. 5(1)(b) and 5(3)
items.quote: any link between the original purpose and the new purpose
items.why: The test when data collected for one purpose is reused for another, such as training a model on customer records. Lists the factors to weigh and the cases treated as compatible (including Annex 2). Article 5(3) adds that compatible processing is not lawful for that reason alone, so a basis is still needed. Inserted by the 2025 Act, s.71(5); in force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(d)).

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How do we ensure lawfulness in AI?
items.locator: Section 'What should we consider when deciding lawful bases?'; also 'How should we distinguish purposes between AI development and deployment?' and 'Can we rely on legitimate interests?'
items.quote: You must break down and separate each distinct processing operation, and identify the purpose and an appropriate lawful basis for each one
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. Says the basis should be decided before processing starts, documented, and not swapped later without good reason; treats development and deployment as separate purposes; goes through each basis for AI. The page carries a banner that it is under review because of the Data (Use and Access) Act and may change; latest update shown is 28 October 2024, so it does not mention recognised legitimate interests.

items.title: Information Commissioner's Office response to the consultation series on generative AI: The lawful basis for web scraping to train generative AI models
items.quote: Legitimate interests remains the sole available lawful basis for training generative AI models using web-scraped personal data based on current practices.
items.why: The regulator's settled position after consultation: only legitimate interests is realistically available for web-scraped training data, developers must show why other ways of collecting data will not do, and poor transparency makes the balancing test hard to pass. The page shows no date; an ICO blog of 12 December 2024 announces the report. Written before the 2025 Act; the ICO says its guidance will be updated to reflect it.

items.title: Legitimate interests: What is the 'legitimate interests' basis?
items.quote: It’s not enough for you to simply say that using personal information is in your legitimate interests.
items.why: The three-part test (purpose, necessity, balancing), which must be satisfied before the information is used. Updated 23 March 2026 for the 2025 Act. The companion chapter 'When can we rely on legitimate interests?' says the basis cannot be the default for everything; 'What else do we need to consider?' says a changed purpose calls for a compatibility check and a fresh assessment.

items.title: A guide to lawful basis: Recognised legitimate interest
items.locator: 'At a glance' and section 'When can we use recognised legitimate interest?'
items.quote: You can’t use recognised legitimate interest as your lawful basis if you want to make significant decisions about someone based solely on automated processing.
items.why: The regulator's plain-language account of the new basis: five conditions with pre-approved public-interest purposes, no balancing test but necessity still required, not available to public authorities performing their tasks, and not usable for solely automated significant decisions. Published 23 March 2026.

items.title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
items.locator: Paras 60 and 66; executive summary pp. 2 to 3 (three-step test; scenarios on unlawfully trained models)
items.quote: the GDPR does not establish any hierarchy between the different legal bases laid down in Article 6(1) GDPR
items.why: EU comparator, not binding in the UK. Applies the same three-step legitimate interest test to developing and deploying AI models, and says a deployer should check that a model it uses was not built by unlawfully processing personal data. Useful for groups operating in both jurisdictions.

items.title: Monetary Penalty Notice: Clearview AI Inc
items.locator: Para 3 (amount), para 4(ii) and para 68 (p. 29) on lawful basis
items.quote: The amount of the penalty is £7,552,800
items.why: Source of the figure. Enforcement on scraped images used for a facial recognition service; one of the listed infringements is the absence of any Article 6 basis. Not a generative AI training case. Status: the First-tier Tribunal set the notice aside on jurisdiction; the Upper Tribunal reversed that on 6 October 2025 ([2025] UKUT 319 (AAC)) and sent the case back; the ICO's news page records permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal on 19 December 2025. The penalty is therefore not final.
